L24@P5-6: 2 GETTING STARTEDCHAPTER
L25@P6: ONE
L26@P6: WHAT IS NUMPY?
L27@P6: NumPy is the fundamental package for scientific computing in Python. It is a Python library that provides a multidimensional array object, various derived objects (such as masked arrays and matrices), and an assortment of routines for
L28@P6: fast operations on arrays, including mathematical, logical, shape manipulation, sorting, selecting, I/O, discrete Fourier
L29@P6: transforms, basic linear algebra, basic statistical operations, random simulation and much more.
L30@P6: At the core of the NumPy package, is the ndarray object. This encapsulates n-dimensional arrays of homogeneous data
L31@P6: types, with many operations being performed in compiled code for performance. There are several important differences
L32@P6: between NumPy arrays and the standard Python sequences:
L33@P6: • NumPy arrays have a fixed size at creation, unlike Python lists (which can grow dynamically). Changing the size
L34@P6: of an ndarray will create a new array and delete the original.
L35@P6: • The elements in a NumPy array are all required to be of the same data type, and thus will be the same size in
L36@P6: memory. The exception: one can have arrays of (Python, including NumPy) objects, thereby allowing for arrays
L37@P6: of different sized elements.
L38@P6: • NumPy arrays facilitate advanced mathematical and other types of operations on large numbers of data. Typically,
L39@P6: such operations are executed more efficiently and with less code than is possible using Python’s built-in sequences.
L40@P6: • A growing plethora of scientific and mathematical Python-based packages are using NumPy arrays; though these
L41@P6: typically support Python-sequence input, they convert such input to NumPy arrays prior to processing, and they
L42@P6: often output NumPy arrays. In other words, in order to efficiently use much (perhaps even most) of today’s scientific/mathematical Python-based software, just knowing how to use Python’s built-in sequence types is insufficient
L43@P6: - one also needs to know how to use NumPy arrays.
L44@P6: The points about sequence size and speed are particularly important in scientific computing. As a simple example,
L45@P6: consider the case of multiplying each element in a 1-D sequence with the corresponding element in another sequence of
L46@P6: the same length. If the data are stored in two Python lists, a and b, we could iterate over each element:
L47@P6: c = []
L48@P6: for i in range(len(a)):
L49@P6: c.append(a[i]*b[i])
L50@P6: This produces the correct answer, but if a and b each contain millions of numbers, we will pay the price for the inefficiencies of looping in Python. We could accomplish the same task much more quickly in C by writing (for clarity we
L51@P6: neglect variable declarations and initializations, memory allocation, etc.)
L52@P6: for (i = 0; i < rows; i++) {
L53@P6: c[i] = a[i]*b[i];
L54@P6: }
L55@P6: This saves all the overhead involved in interpreting the Python code and manipulating Python objects, but at the expense
L56@P6: of the benefits gained from coding in Python. Furthermore, the coding work required increases with the dimensionality
L57@P6: of our data. In the case of a 2-D array, for example, the C code (abridged as before) expands to
L58@P6-7: 3NumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L59@P7: for (i = 0; i < rows; i++) {
L60@P7: for (j = 0; j < columns; j++) {
L61@P7: c[i][j] = a[i][j]*b[i][j];
L62@P7: }
L63@P7: }
L64@P7: NumPy gives us the best of both worlds: element-by-element operations are the “default mode” when an ndarray is
L65@P7: involved, but the element-by-element operation is speedily executed by pre-compiled C code. In NumPy
L66@P7: c = a * b
L67@P7: does what the earlier examples do, at near-C speeds, but with the code simplicity we expect from something based on
L68@P7: Python. Indeed, the NumPy idiom is even simpler! This last example illustrates two of NumPy’s features which are the
L69@P7: basis of much of its power: vectorization and broadcasting.
L70@P7: 1.1 Why is NumPy fast?
L71@P7: Vectorization describes the absence of any explicit looping, indexing, etc., in the code - these things are taking place, of
L72@P7: course, just “behind the scenes” in optimized, pre-compiled C code. Vectorized code has many advantages, among which
L73@P7: are:
L74@P7: • vectorized code is more concise and easier to read
L75@P7: • fewer lines of code generally means fewer bugs
L76@P7: • the code more closely resembles standard mathematical notation (making it easier, typically, to correctly code
L77@P7: mathematical constructs)
L78@P7: • vectorization results in more “Pythonic” code. Without vectorization, our code would be littered with inefficient
L79@P7: and difficult to read for loops.
L80@P7: Broadcasting is the term used to describe the implicit element-by-element behavior of operations; generally speaking,
L81@P7: in NumPy all operations, not just arithmetic operations, but logical, bit-wise, functional, etc., behave in this implicit
L82@P7: element-by-element fashion, i.e., they broadcast. Moreover, in the example above, a and b could be multidimensional
L83@P7: arrays of the same shape, or a scalar and an array, or even two arrays with different shapes, provided that the smaller array
L84@P7: is “expandable” to the shape of the larger in such a way that the resulting broadcast is unambiguous. For detailed “rules”
L85@P7: of broadcasting see Broadcasting.
L86@P7: 1.2 Who else uses NumPy?
L87@P7: NumPy fully supports an object-oriented approach, starting, once again, with ndarray. For example, ndarray is a
L88@P7: class, possessing numerous methods and attributes. Many of its methods are mirrored by functions in the outer-most
L89@P7: NumPy namespace, allowing the programmer to code in whichever paradigm they prefer. This flexibility has allowed the
L90@P7: NumPy array dialect and NumPy ndarray class to become the de-facto language of multi-dimensional data interchange
L91@P7: used in Python.
L92@P7-8: 4 1. What is NumPy?CHAPTER
L93@P8: TWO
L94@P8: NUMPY QUICKSTART
L95@P8: 2.1 Prerequisites
L96@P8: You’ll need to know a bit of Python. For a refresher, see the Python tutorial.
L97@P8: To work the examples, you’ll need matplotlib installed in addition to NumPy.
L98@P8: Learner profile
L99@P8: This is a quick overview of arrays in NumPy. It demonstrates how n-dimensional (n >= 2) arrays are represented and
L100@P8: can be manipulated. In particular, if you don’t know how to apply common functions to n-dimensional arrays (without
L101@P8: using for-loops), or if you want to understand axis and shape properties for n-dimensional arrays, this article might be of
L102@P8: help.
L103@P8: Learning Objectives
L104@P8: After reading, you should be able to:
L105@P8: • Understand the difference between one-, two- and n-dimensional arrays in NumPy;
L106@P8: • Understand how to apply some linear algebra operations to n-dimensional arrays without using for-loops;
L107@P8: • Understand axis and shape properties for n-dimensional arrays.
L108@P8: 2.2 The basics
L109@P8: NumPy’s main object is the homogeneous multidimensional array. It is a table of elements (usually numbers), all of the
L110@P8: same type, indexed by a tuple of non-negative integers. In NumPy dimensions are called axes.
L111@P8: For example, the array for the coordinates of a point in 3D space, [1, 2, 1], has one axis. That axis has 3 elements
L112@P8: in it, so we say it has a length of 3. In the example pictured below, the array has 2 axes. The first axis has a length of 2,
L113@P8: the second axis has a length of 3.
L114@P8: [[1., 0., 0.],
L115@P8: [0., 1., 2.]]
L116@P8: NumPy’s array class is called ndarray. It is also known by the alias array. Note that numpy.array is not the
L117@P8: same as the Standard Python Library class array.array, which only handles one-dimensional arrays and offers less
L118@P8: functionality. The more important attributes of an ndarray object are:
L119@P8: ndarray.ndim
L120@P8: the number of axes (dimensions) of the array.
L121@P8: ndarray.shape
L122@P8: the dimensions of the array. This is a tuple of integers indicating the size of the array in each dimension. For a
L123@P8-9: 5NumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L124@P9: matrix with n rows and m columns, shape will be (n,m). The length of the shape tuple is therefore the number
L125@P9: of axes, ndim.
L126@P9: ndarray.size
L127@P9: the total number of elements of the array. This is equal to the product of the elements of shape.
L128@P9: ndarray.dtype
L129@P9: an object describing the type of the elements in the array. One can create or specify dtype’s using standard Python
L130@P9: types. Additionally NumPy provides types of its own. numpy.int32, numpy.int16, and numpy.float64 are some
L131@P9: examples.
L132@P9: ndarray.itemsize
L133@P9: the size in bytes of each element of the array. For example, an array of elements of type float64 has itemsize
L134@P9: 8 (=64/8), while one of type complex32 has itemsize 4 (=32/8). It is equivalent to ndarray.dtype.
L135@P9: itemsize.
L136@P9: ndarray.data
L137@P9: the buffer containing the actual elements of the array. Normally, we won’t need to use this attribute because we
L138@P9: will access the elements in an array using indexing facilities.
L139@P9: 2.2.1 An example
L140@P9: >>> import numpy as np
L141@P9: >>> a = np.arange(15).reshape(3, 5)
L142@P9: >>> a
L143@P9: array([[ 0, 1, 2, 3, 4],
L144@P9: [ 5, 6, 7, 8, 9],
L145@P9: [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]])
L146@P9: >>> a.shape
L147@P9: (3, 5)
L148@P9: >>> a.ndim
L149@P9: 2
L150@P9: >>> a.dtype.name
L151@P9: 'int64'
L152@P9: >>> a.itemsize
L153@P9: 8
L154@P9: >>> a.size
L155@P9: 15
L156@P9: >>> type(a)
L157@P9: <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
L158@P9: >>> b = np.array([6, 7, 8])
L159@P9: >>> b
L160@P9: array([6, 7, 8])
L161@P9: >>> type(b)
L162@P9: <class 'numpy.ndarray'>

L164@P10: 2.2.2 Array creation
L165@P10: There are several ways to create arrays.
L166@P10: For example, you can create an array from a regular Python list or tuple using the array function. The type of the
L167@P10: resulting array is deduced from the type of the elements in the sequences.
L168@P10: >>> import numpy as np
L169@P10: >>> a = np.array([2, 3, 4])
L170@P10: >>> a
L171@P10: array([2, 3, 4])
L172@P10: >>> a.dtype
L173@P10: dtype('int64')
L174@P10: >>> b = np.array([1.2, 3.5, 5.1])
L175@P10: >>> b.dtype
L176@P10: dtype('float64')
L177@P10: A frequent error consists in calling array with multiple arguments, rather than providing a single sequence as an argument.
L178@P10: >>> a = np.array(1, 2, 3, 4) # WRONG
L179@P10: Traceback (most recent call last):
L180@P10: ...
L181@P10: TypeError: array() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 4 were given
L182@P10: >>> a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) # RIGHT
L183@P10: array transforms sequences of sequences into two-dimensional arrays, sequences of sequences of sequences into threedimensional arrays, and so on.
L184@P10: >>> b = np.array([(1.5, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6)])
L185@P10: >>> b
L186@P10: array([[1.5, 2. , 3. ],
L187@P10: [4. , 5. , 6. ]])
L188@P10: The type of the array can also be explicitly specified at creation time:
L189@P10: >>> c = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]], dtype=np.complex128)
L190@P10: >>> c
L191@P10: array([[1.+0.j, 2.+0.j],
L192@P10: [3.+0.j, 4.+0.j]])
L193@P10: Often, the elements of an array are originally unknown, but its size is known. Hence, NumPy offers several functions to
L194@P10: create arrays with initial placeholder content. These minimize the necessity of growing arrays, an expensive operation.
L195@P10: The function zeros creates an array full of zeros, the function ones creates an array full of ones, and the function
L196@P10: empty creates an array whose initial content is random and depends on the state of the memory. By default, the dtype
L197@P10: of the created array is float64, but it can be specified via the key word argument dtype.
L198@P10: >>> np.zeros((3, 4))
L199@P10: array([[0., 0., 0., 0.],
L200@P10: [0., 0., 0., 0.],
L201@P10: [0., 0., 0., 0.]])
L202@P10: >>> np.ones((2, 3, 4), dtype=np.int16)
L203@P10: array([[[1, 1, 1, 1],
L204@P10: [1, 1, 1, 1],
L205@P10: [1, 1, 1, 1]],
L206@P10: [[1, 1, 1, 1],
L207@P10: (continues on next page)
L208@P10-11: 2.2. The basics 7NumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L209@P11: (continued from previous page)
L210@P11: [1, 1, 1, 1],
L211@P11: [1, 1, 1, 1]]], dtype=int16)
L212@P11: >>> np.empty((2, 3))
L213@P11: array([[3.73603959e-262, 6.02658058e-154, 6.55490914e-260], # may vary
L214@P11: [5.30498948e-313, 3.14673309e-307, 1.00000000e+000]])
L215@P11: To create sequences of numbers, NumPy provides the arange function which is analogous to the Python built-in range,
L216@P11: but returns an array.
L217@P11: >>> np.arange(10, 30, 5)
L218@P11: array([10, 15, 20, 25])
L219@P11: >>> np.arange(0, 2, 0.3) # it accepts float arguments
L220@P11: array([0. , 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2, 1.5, 1.8])
L221@P11: When arange is used with floating point arguments, it is generally not possible to predict the number of elements
L222@P11: obtained, due to the finite floating point precision. For this reason, it is usually better to use the function linspace that
L223@P11: receives as an argument the number of elements that we want, instead of the step:
L224@P11: >>> from numpy import pi
L225@P11: >>> np.linspace(0, 2, 9) # 9 numbers from 0 to 2
L226@P11: array([0. , 0.25, 0.5 , 0.75, 1. , 1.25, 1.5 , 1.75, 2. ])
L227@P11: >>> x = np.linspace(0, 2 * pi, 100) # useful to evaluate function at lots of␣
L228@P11: ,→points
L229@P11: >>> f = np.sin(x)
L230@P11: See also:
L231@P11: array, zeros, zeros_like, ones, ones_like, empty, empty_like, arange, linspace, random.
L232@P11: Generator.random, random.Generator.normal, fromfunction, fromfile
L233@P11: 2.2.3 Printing arrays
L234@P11: When you print an array, NumPy displays it in a similar way to nested lists, but with the following layout:
L235@P11: • the last axis is printed from left to right,
L236@P11: • the second-to-last is printed from top to bottom,
L237@P11: • the rest are also printed from top to bottom, with each slice separated from the next by an empty line.
L238@P11: One-dimensional arrays are then printed as rows, bidimensionals as matrices and tridimensionals as lists of matrices.
L239@P11: >>> a = np.arange(6) # 1d array
L240@P11: >>> print(a)
L241@P11: [0 1 2 3 4 5]
L242@P11: >>>
L243@P11: >>> b = np.arange(12).reshape(4, 3) # 2d array
L244@P11: >>> print(b)
L245@P11: [[ 0 1 2]
L246@P11: [ 3 4 5]
L247@P11: [ 6 7 8]
L248@P11: [ 9 10 11]]
L249@P11: >>>
L250@P11: >>> c = np.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4) # 3d array
L251@P11: >>> print(c)
L252@P11: [[[ 0 1 2 3]
L253@P11: [ 4 5 6 7]
L254@P11: (continues on next page)
L255@P11-12: 8 2. NumPy quickstartNumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L256@P12: (continued from previous page)
L257@P12: [ 8 9 10 11]]
L258@P12: [[12 13 14 15]
L259@P12: [16 17 18 19]
L260@P12: [20 21 22 23]]]
L261@P12: See below to get more details on reshape.
L262@P12: If an array is too large to be printed, NumPy automatically skips the central part of the array and only prints the corners:
L263@P12: >>> print(np.arange(10000))
L264@P12: [ 0 1 2 ... 9997 9998 9999]
L265@P12: >>>
L266@P12: >>> print(np.arange(10000).reshape(100, 100))
L267@P12: [[ 0 1 2 ... 97 98 99]
L268@P12: [ 100 101 102 ... 197 198 199]
L269@P12: [ 200 201 202 ... 297 298 299]
L270@P12: ...

L277@P12: 2.2.4 Basic operations
L278@P12: Arithmetic operators on arrays apply elementwise. A new array is created and filled with the result.
L279@P12: >>> a = np.array([20, 30, 40, 50])
L280@P12: >>> b = np.arange(4)
L281@P12: >>> b
L282@P12: array([0, 1, 2, 3])
L283@P12: >>> c = a - b
L284@P12: >>> c
L285@P12: array([20, 29, 38, 47])
L286@P12: >>> b**2
L287@P12: array([0, 1, 4, 9])
L288@P12: >>> 10 * np.sin(a)
L289@P12: array([ 9.12945251, -9.88031624, 7.4511316 , -2.62374854])
L290@P12: >>> a < 35
L291@P12: array([ True, True, False, False])
L292@P12: Unlike in many matrix languages, the product operator * operates elementwise in NumPy arrays. The matrix product
L293@P12: can be performed using the @ operator (in python >=3.5) or the dot function or method:
L294@P12: >>> A = np.array([[1, 1],
L295@P12: ... [0, 1]])
L296@P12: >>> B = np.array([[2, 0],
L297@P12: ... [3, 4]])
L298@P12: >>> A * B # elementwise product
L299@P12: array([[2, 0],
L300@P12: [0, 4]])
L301@P12: (continues on next page)
L302@P12-13: 2.2. The basics 9NumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L303@P13: (continued from previous page)
L304@P13: >>> A @ B # matrix product
L305@P13: array([[5, 4],
L306@P13: [3, 4]])
L307@P13: >>> A.dot(B) # another matrix product
L308@P13: array([[5, 4],
L309@P13: [3, 4]])
L310@P13: Some operations, such as += and *=, act in place to modify an existing array rather than create a new one.
L311@P13: >>> rg = np.random.default_rng(1) # create instance of default random number␣
L312@P13: ,→generator
L313@P13: >>> a = np.ones((2, 3), dtype=np.int_)
L314@P13: >>> b = rg.random((2, 3))

L316@P13: >>> a
L317@P13: array([[3, 3, 3],
L318@P13: [3, 3, 3]])

L320@P13: >>> b
L321@P13: array([[3.51182162, 3.9504637 , 3.14415961],
L322@P13: [3.94864945, 3.31183145, 3.42332645]])

L329@P13: one (a behavior known as upcasting).
L330@P13: >>> a = np.ones(3, dtype=np.int32)

L378@P14: 2.2.5 Universal functions
L379@P14: NumPy provides familiar mathematical functions such as sin, cos, and exp. In NumPy, these are called “universal functions” (ufunc). Within NumPy, these functions operate elementwise on an array, producing an array as output.
L380@P14: >>> B = np.arange(3)
L381@P14: >>> B
L382@P14: array([0, 1, 2])
L383@P14: >>> np.exp(B)
L384@P14: array([1. , 2.71828183, 7.3890561 ])
L385@P14: >>> np.sqrt(B)
L386@P14: array([0. , 1. , 1.41421356])
